newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court considers death-row inmate's case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court considers death-row inmate's case.

text.p: An attorney for convicted murderer Joseph O'Dell asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to overturn his death sentence because the prosecutor told the jury he might commit more crimes if given a lesser sentence.

Attorney Robert Smith accused the prosecutor of "scaring the jury about a dangerous man being back on the streets" without telling them O'Dell could be sentenced under existing law to life in prison without parole if they did not vote for the death penalty.
Katherine Baldwin, a state assistant attorney general, defended the prosecutor's remarks as proper and told the high court "Virginia should be permitted to carry out the sentence in this case."

O'Dell's case has been publicised by death penalty opponents on the Internet. Pope John Paul II heard about it in Italy from an advertisement by the Amnesty International human rights group and the case has sparked street protests in Rome.
O'Dell also has claimed new DNA evidence casts doubt on his 1986 conviction for raping and murdering a 44-year-old secretary from Virginia Beach, Virginia.

But the Supreme Court during the hour-long arguments did not address O'Dell's guilt or innocence, considering only whether the jury should have been told he could get life in prison without parole as an alternative to the death sentence.

Smith said the prosecutor was attempting to frighten the sentencing jury by warning that O'Dell would be dangerous if released from prison. He said O'Dell should have been able to reply, "I'm going to be locked up for the rest of my life."

But several justices questioned how such an assurance could be made, noting that a state always may change parole conditions to allow for the release of certain inmates. "Laws can change," Justice Anthony Kennedy said.

Under questioning, Smith admitted that O'Dell did tell the jury he was 45 years old, and with the expected prison term "I ain't never going to get out." But he did not specifically say he could get life in prison without parole.

Arguing for the state, Baldwin denied that the prosecutor improperly misled the jury while urging the death penalty and listing O'Dell long criminal history. "There has never been a claim of improper prosecutorial argument," she said.

But Justice David Souter said the prosecutor's remarks left the impression with the jury that O'Dell could be paroled from prison and commit more crimes. Justice Stephen Breyer said it conveyed a "serious misapprehension" to the jury by suggesting that a life sentence "doesn't mean life" and therefore O'Dell should be sentenced to death.
Baldwin said there should be "finality of judgments" in urging that O'Dell's death sentence be upheld.
The Supreme Court after the arguments took the case under advisement, with a decision expected before July.
